uganda.investigationNote: Uganda is the first country run through the policy evidence pipeline (editor sequencing: Uganda -> Rwanda -> Tanzania -> regional comparison). Six pillars attempted; data protection landed strongest (regulator decision + statute anchors); licensing partially verified pending UCC instruments; energy/construction/environmental not yet attempted and recorded as pillar gaps rather than unverified claims.

claims.statement: Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 (now revised as Cap. 97) was assented to on 25 February 2019 and commenced on 3 May 2019, with its implementing Regulations effective 12 March 2021.
claims.note: Official depository metadata (ULII) and DLA Piper handbook agree. Conflict resolved: Legal500 states commencement 1 March 2019 - rejected as a secondary-source error; the gazette date 3 May 2019 controls.

claims.statement: The Act applies extraterritorially: it covers a person, institution or public body outside Uganda who collects, processes, holds or uses personal data relating to Ugandan citizens (s.1).
claims.note: CIPESA quotes the statutory text; DLA Piper reports the PDPO's own confirmation. Statute text capture-pending (ULII gate) - state self-upgrades on full-text capture.

claims.statement: Every data collector, processor or controller must register with the Personal Data Protection Office (s.29) and renew registration annually; the duty applies to foreign entities handling Ugandans' personal data until an exemption is gazetted.
claims.note: Duty-level claim verified by two independent reports of the PDPO decision and the statute. Fee/portal mechanics deliberately split into UG-DP-C4 (weaker evidence).

claims.statement: Registration is completed online via the PDPO portal (Form 2 application plus Form 3 cross-border undertaking), fee UGX 100,000, typically 4-7 working days for initial registration.
claims.note: Single Tier-3 source; the PDPO portal itself (pdpo.go.ug/register) was unreachable on 2026-09-22. Verify fees/SLA against the portal or the Regulations before citing operationally. Editorial ruling 2026-09-22 (delegated): kept split from UG-DP-C3 - the legal duty and the operational mechanics have different evidence bases and upgrade paths; folding would misdescribe the duty's verified position.

claims.statement: Cross-border transfer or storage of personal data outside Uganda requires either data-subject consent or adequate protection in the recipient country at least equivalent to the Act (s.19); no advance approval per transfer is required, but records of the legal basis and safeguards must be maintained and produced on audit.
claims.note: s.19 text quoted by CIPESA; the no-pre-approval clarification is the PDPO's own position reported by DLA Piper. Material to colocation operators serving cross-border workloads (e.g. Kampala-Nairobi replication paths).

claims.statement: In a decision of 18 July 2025 (Ssekamwa Frank & 3 Others v Google LLC, Complaint No. 08/11/24/6683), the PDPO found Google LLC in breach of ss.29 and 19 and ordered registration, designation of a data protection officer, and production of a cross-border transfer compliance framework within 30 days - confirming the Act reaches foreign entities with no physical presence in Uganda.
claims.note: Primary instrument (the decision itself) is capture-pending - not published on the regulator site; two independent reports agree on the findings and the complaint number. If either report is later contradicted, this claim degrades.

claims.statement: The Uganda Communications Commission's statutory mandate covers telecommunications, broadcasting, radio communication, postal communications, data communication and infrastructure.
claims.note: Captured from the official UCC page itself.

claims.statement: Uganda's technology-neutral licensing framework (introduced 2019/2020 under the Uganda Communications (Licensing) Regulations, 2019) replaced the earlier PIP/PSP classes with principal categories including National Telecom Operator (NTO), National Public Service Provider (NPSP), Regional Public Service Provider (RPSP) and Regional Public Infrastructure Provider (RPIP), plus authorisations for capacity resale and value-added services.
claims.note: Licence classes rest on one Tier-3 guide; the definitive UCC instrument (Description of Telecom Licenses and Authorisations) is capture-pending. Upgrade path: fetch the instrument or the Regulations text.

claims.statement: Infrastructure companies building data-centre assets for use by licensed operators fall within UCC's licensing regime and must apply for the matching licence class.
claims.note: The claim most material to directory operators (Raxio UG1 et al.). Currently single-source (Tier 3). UCC's own instrument is capture-pending; also check Raxio's regulatory/registration disclosures. Editor attention requested before publication. Editorial ruling 2026-09-22: publication hold applied (see publicationHold).
claims.publicationHold: Editor ruling 2026-09-22 (delegated): do NOT cite publicly - not even with state attribution - until a Tier 1/2 UCC instrument (Description of Telecom Licenses and Authorisations or the Licensing Regulations text) confirms it. A licensing-requirement claim that later proves wrong creates compliance misinformation for readers and operators; silence is the safer failure mode.

claims.statement: UCC licence applications require Ugandan legal personality, a physical business address, a Tax Identification Number with tax clearance, and demonstrated financial and technical capacity (business/technical plans, audited financials or capitalisation proof).
claims.note: Single Tier-3 guide referencing the official UCC requirements document; instrument capture-pending.

claims.statement: Uganda's Digital Transformation Roadmap (FY2023/24-2027/28) lists development of reliable digital infrastructure - including high-speed broadband networks, data centres and cloud computing capabilities - as a priority.
claims.note: Official government domain snippet explicitly names data centres; full document fetch gated. Direct official mention of data-centre infrastructure - upgrade on PDF capture.

claims.statement: The Digital Uganda Vision (DUV) is the overarching 20-year ICT development framework aligned to Uganda Vision 2040, harmonising the country's ICT policies.
claims.note: Official NITA-U framing captured from snippet; strategy page fetch gated.

claims.statement: Investors in Uganda can access tax incentives through the Uganda Investment Authority and the Uganda Free Zones Authority, including a 10-year income tax holiday for qualifying foreign investment.
claims.note: Non-Ugandan official assessment (Tier 3 for our purposes); UIA/UFZA primary instruments not yet captured. No data-centre-specific incentive verified - any DC-specific treatment remains unverified.

rwanda.investigationNote: Second country through the policy pipeline. Evidence quality higher than Uganda's round because the Tier-1 instruments were directly fetchable: RURA licensing regulation full text (59pp PDF), Law 058/2021 official gazette text (82pp PDF), DPO services site, RDB incentive page. 11 of 13 claims verified from verbatim instrument text; the two partially-verified claims rest on snippet-level official sources. Material differences vs Uganda now anchored at Tier 1: prior authorisation for cross-border transfer (Art. 48) and default in-country storage (Art. 50) vs Uganda's records-based s.19 regime; explicit DC licence class with tiered fees vs Uganda's unnamed-category ambiguity.

claims.statement: RURA Regulation No 013/R/EC-ICT/RURA/2021 of 25/02/2021 governs licensing in Rwanda's electronic communications sector and came into force on the day of its publication in the Official Gazette.
claims.note: Full official PDF captured (59pp): 'Article 48: Commencement - This regulation comes into force on the day of its publication in the official gazette'; signed Kigali 25/02/2021 (Dr Ignace Gatare, Chairperson of the Regulatory Board).

claims.statement: The Regulation issues licences in three categories - network infrastructure, network services, and application services (Art. 9) - through three types: individual licences (issued by auction to a National Telecommunication Operator), standard licences, and general authorisations (Art. 6-8).
claims.note: Verbatim from captured text: 'The Regulatory Authority issues the licenses to operators who provide the following services: 1. Network infrastructure; 2. Network services; and 3. Application services.'

claims.statement: Data centres are an explicitly named licence class in Rwanda: under Annex One Category 3 (Application Service Providers), a data centre not holding an ISP or NTO licence pays USD 100 application / USD 2,000 licence fee on a standard 5-year licence (facility Tiers One and Two), or USD 1,000 / USD 10,000 on a standard 15-year licence (facility Tiers Three and Four and plus).
claims.note: The claim Uganda's dataset could not yet verify at Tier 1 (cf. UG-LC-C3, on publication hold). Rwanda's regulator names data centres in the fee schedule with tier-differentiated pricing. Operator-material: ADC Kigali KGL1 and any future Rwanda records fall here. Fee amounts as printed in the captured PDF; re-verify against current RURA schedule before advising on costs.

claims.statement: Network Infrastructure Provider licensees must own, operate or provide any form of active or passive physical infrastructure used for carrying or providing services, applications and content (Art. 10).
claims.note: Verbatim captured. Context for colocation/interconnection analysis: passive infrastructure (ducts, dark fibre) sits inside the licensed scope.

claims.statement: Rwanda's data protection law is Law No 058/2021 of 13/10/2021 relating to the protection of personal data and privacy, officially gazetted on 15 October 2021.
claims.note: Official gazette PDF captured (82pp bilingual, header 'Official Gazette n° Special of 15/10/2021'); RISA page and DataGuidance corroborate.

claims.statement: A person who intends to be a data controller or a data processor must register with the supervisory authority (Art. 29).
claims.note: Verbatim captured. Practice detail: registration administered through the NCSA/DPO; transitional compliance window ended 15 October 2023 (RW-DP-C6).

claims.statement: Cross-border sharing or transfer of personal data outside Rwanda is permitted only if the controller/processor has (1) obtained authorisation from the supervisory authority after providing proof of appropriate safeguards, or (2) the data subject's consent, or (3) necessity grounds (contract performance, public interest, legal claims, vital interests) (Art. 48).
claims.note: Verbatim captured from the official gazette text. MATERIAL DIFFERENCE vs Uganda: Uganda's PDPO confirmed no advance approval is required (records-based regime; UG-DP-C5). Rwanda requires prior authorisation as the first branch.

claims.statement: Personal data must be stored in Rwanda; storage outside Rwanda is only permitted if the controller/processor holds a valid registration certificate authorising storage outside Rwanda, issued by the supervisory authority (Art. 50).
claims.note: Verbatim captured; the DPO's official services menu ('Authorization to Store Outside Rwanda') corroborates operationally. MATERIAL DIFFERENCE vs Uganda: no equivalent default-localisation provision captured in Uganda's Act. Direct colocation-demand driver for in-country Rwandan facilities.

claims.statement: The National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA) is the designated supervisory authority under the Data Protection Law, and the Data Protection and Privacy Office (DPO) administers registration and authorisations under it.
claims.note: DataGuidance names NCSA as designated supervisory authority; the official DPO site shows registration 'with NCSA' and the authorisation services. The law text itself uses the generic term 'supervisory authority'.

claims.statement: The transitional period for data controller/processor registration ended on 15 October 2023, after which registration became mandatory without the transition window.
claims.note: Official NCSA page captured only as search snippet (shell on fetch); deadline corroborated by DLA Piper Africa briefing. Upgrade on full NCSA page capture.

claims.statement: A registered investor investing at least USD 50,000,000 (with at least 30% equity) in qualifying sectors - including Information and Communication Technology (excluding ICT retail/wholesale trade, ICT repair, and telecommunications) - is entitled to a corporate income tax holiday of up to seven years.
claims.note: Verbatim captured from RDB's official One Stop Centre page. A large data-centre campus could qualify under ICT, but 'telecommunications' exclusion needs care for operator-affiliated facilities - interpretation deferred to the article layer.

claims.statement: An international company with its headquarters or regional office in Rwanda is entitled to a 0% preferential corporate income tax rate if it invests at least USD 10,000,000 in tangible and intangible assets and provides employment and training to Rwandans.
claims.note: Verbatim captured. Regional-HQ path relevant to pan-African DC operators choosing Kigali.

claims.statement: Rwanda's ICT Sector Strategic Plan (2024-2029) aligns with the Smart Rwanda Master Plan (SRMP II) and its core pillars (Digital Business, Digital Citizen), under the 30-year Vision 2050 agenda.
claims.note: Official-domain snippets only (minict.gov.rw / minecofin.gov.rw); SSP PDF capture pending. Any explicit 'data centre' language in the SSP awaits full-text capture.

publicationPolicy.verified: may be cited as fact in the interpretation layer (articles, profiles)
publicationPolicy.partially-verified: may be cited only with visible state attribution ('per one TMT practice guide; official instrument pending'); numeric/compliance-sensitive partially-verified claims should not carry operational weight
publicationPolicy.capture-pending: state reserved for claims whose evidence chain is blocked by an inaccessible source
publicationPolicy.unverified: not published as fact; may appear as an open question
publicationPolicy.contradicted: not published as fact; the conflict is explained if referenced
publicationPolicy.publicationHold: per-claim hold override: block all public citation regardless of state; used where a claim's failure mode creates real-world compliance risk (applies to UG-LC-C3)

gapSchema.rule: A pillar with no research yet is recorded as a structured gap - never as an unverified claim. Each gap names expected instruments/regulators and its upgrade path. Gaps are reviewed for staleness at every datasetVersion bump (editor ruling 2026-09-22).
